clue.text: Scottish philosopher without a name for being sympathetic

indicators.note: without here has its old sense of outside, so the philosopher wraps around the other piece

blocks.note: David Hume, the Edinburgh philosopher of the Enlightenment
a is A and N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A Scottish thinker is praised for his kindness despite having no name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it has its old sense of outside, as in the hymn's 'a green hill far away, without a city wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone humane shows compassion and kindness towards others, which is what a sympathetic person does.

clue.text: A form of restraint for workers embracing strike

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: hands are manual workers, as in farm hands
to cuff is to strike with the open hand

explanation.surface: Workers on a picket line are kept in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action alongside workers, but it is a blow: HAND(CUFF)S.
explanation.definitionFit: Handcuffs are a linked pair of metal rings locked round a prisoner's wrists to stop free movement.

clue.text: Mission in confusion, period!

blocks.note: a mess is a state of disorder
an age is a period of history

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that a whole mission is chaos, full stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Period!' sounds like the American full stop of emphasis, but it is just a span of time.
explanation.definitionFit: In older usage a message is an errand or task one is sent on, which is what a mission is.

clue.text: A strange thing, to change to work in unsocial hours

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the next word's letters are made odd

blocks.note: taken as written
to shift is to change or move

explanation.surface: Something odd changes how people work at antisocial times.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'A' just reads into the sentence; only the five letters of thing are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A night shift is a period of employment through the hours of darkness, when most people sleep.

clue.text: After a period rabble is repulsed, initially by an explosive device

indicators.note: something repulsed is driven back, so the word for rabble is written backwards
initially points to the opening letter only of the word that follows it

blocks.note: a period is a stretch of time
a rabble is a disorderly crowd, a mob
the first letter of by

explanation.surface: After some time an unruly crowd is beaten back, at first by a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a period' tells you the order: the period piece comes first and everything else follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A time bomb is a bomb set with a timer to go off later, so it is literally an explosive device.

clue.text: Edmund II's warship

blocks.note: Edmund II, king of England in 1016, was known as Ironside
the possessive ending, taken as written

explanation.surface: A question of which ship belonged to an English king.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Ironsides is the nickname of USS Constitution; the king's nickname plus the possessive s gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Ironsides is the famous nickname of the American frigate USS Constitution, a fighting ship of 1797.

clue.text: At the end of the day it's equally balanced

definitions.text: At the end of the day

blocks.clueFragment: At the end of the day
blocks.note: first meaning: a poetic word for ...
second meaning: level, with neither side ahead

explanation.surface: When all is said and done, the situation is fair to both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' reads as the cliché meaning 'ultimately', but it means evening literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Even is an archaic poetic form of evening, as in eventide, and also means level or fifty-fifty.

clue.text: Cheering eggs it on, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals the words before it are one possible arrangement, so their letters may be shuffled

blocks.note: ova is Latin for eggs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crowd's applause urges a performer on, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eggs it on' looks like the phrase meaning encourages, but eggs gives OVA.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovation is a burst of loud applause and cheers from an audience, often standing.

clue.text: Fight in the battalion for the Colour

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: Bn is the military abbreviation for battalion
a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A battalion fights to defend its regimental flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colour' suggests a regiment's flag, which suits the battalion, but here it is just a shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown is a shade of the spectrum, the hue of earth or wood.

clue.text: Old court associated with Rochester?

blocks.note: first meaning: a medieval circuit court of travelling judges
second meaning: the surname of the heroine who marries Mr Rochester in Charlotte Brontë's novel

explanation.surface: A historic court connected with a cathedral city in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Rochester is a Kent city, but here it is Mr Rochester of Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyre was a medieval English court held by justices in eyre on circuit, and Jane of that name loves Rochester.

clue.text: Lack of authority to accept, for example, flowers

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: having no say means having no power in a decision
e.g. is the usual abbreviation for for example

explanation.surface: A powerless person must accept, say, a bunch of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: To have no say is to have no voice in a decision, which is how lacking authority becomes a two-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small posy of sweet-smelling blooms, so the plural flowers describes what it contains.

clue.text: Herb growing round wild ass's retreat

indicators.note: to retreat is to go back, so the animal's name is read from its end

blocks.note: O is round in shape
the onager is a wild ass of Asia

explanation.surface: A herb grows around the place where a wild donkey shelters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' looks like a noun, the ass's hideaway, but it is a verb telling you to read the animal backwards, after the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is a culinary plant of the mint family, wild marjoram, used to season Mediterranean cooking.

clue.text: Map soldiers employ to find a monastery

blocks.note: a chart is a map, especially one for sailors
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to employ something is to use it

explanation.surface: Soldiers use a map to locate a remote religious house.
explanation.definitionFit: La Grande Chartreuse is the mother house of the Carthusian order near Grenoble, and the name is used for any Carthusian house.

clue.text: Scandinavian drink Mickey introduced

blocks.note: first meaning: a native of Finland
second meaning: the word that follows Mickey in the name of a drugged drink

explanation.surface: Someone from the north slips a drug into a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A Mickey Finn is a drink secretly laced with a knockout drug; Mickey introduces the name, and the second half is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Finn is a person from Finland, loosely grouped with the Nordic peoples, and Finn completes the phrase Mickey Finn.

clue.text: 8's qualification to be a landscape gardener

definitions.text: 8's qualification to be a landscape gardener

blocks.note: surface reading: the credentials Brown had for the job
setter's reading: the nickname that qualifies, or comes before, Brown in the gardener's name

explanation.walkthrough: 8 is BROWN, and Lancelot Brown, the 18th-century designer of English country-house parks, was nicknamed for this word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means ability or competence, a qualification, and it is also the famous nickname of the gardener Brown.

clue.text: Rather forward for an undergraduate

blocks.note: first meaning: more cheeky or impudent, comparative of an adjective
second meaning: a student in the first year at university

explanation.surface: A student is a bit too bold.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh can mean cheeky, so the comparative means somewhat bold; separately a first-year student at college is called this.

clue.text: Policemen once on horseback, taking second place

blocks.note: the Bow Street Runners were London's early police force
a rider is said to be up on the horse

explanation.surface: Mounted police of old finish behind the winners.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is plural like the answer, describing those taking second place.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners-up are those who come second in a contest, just behind the winner.

clue.text: Exhausted, but ran — and died tragically

indicators.note: a tragic turn wrecks things, so the words before it come out in a ruined order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worn-out runner keeps going and then collapses and dies.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'and' only joins the two fodder words; the seven letters of RAN and DIED make DRAINED.
explanation.definitionFit: Drained and exhausted both mean emptied of all energy and strength, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: 30 injured in capsized Russian warship

indicators.note: something injured is damaged out of shape, so the cross-referenced word's letters are jumbled
in puts the jumbled piece inside the other
a capsized boat is turned over, so in a down clue the word is read upwards

blocks.note: 30 refers to the answer to 30 across
Red was the standard word for a Soviet Russian

explanation.surface: Wounded sailors are aboard an overturned Soviet naval vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 30 points to another answer in the grid; solve that clue first, then jumble its letters inside the upturned colour of communism.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is a fast, manoeuvrable naval ship designed to escort fleets and hunt submarines.

clue.text: “____the sinews, summon up the blood” (Hen. V)

blocks.clueFragment: “____the sinews, summon up the blood” (Hen. V)
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with its first word missing
setter's reading: the gap is filled from King Henry's speech before Harfleur

explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Henry's 'Once more unto the breach' speech in Shakespeare's Henry V; the missing word is a verb meaning to make rigid.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs an imperative verb telling soldiers to tense and harden their muscles before attacking.

clue.text: Seventeen-year-old legally supported by a princess

blocks.note: in English law a person under eighteen was an infant, a minor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teenager is legally backed by a royal daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supported by' puts the second piece underneath the first.
explanation.definitionFit: An infanta is a daughter of the king of Spain or Portugal, a royal princess.

clue.text: Strike-breakers around Burlington House are six-footers

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped about the other

blocks.note: scab is a contemptuous word for a worker who breaks a strike
Burlington House on Piccadilly is home of the Royal Academy, RA

explanation.surface: Strike-breakers gather outside a London building and turn out to be very tall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footers' suggests tall people, but insects have six feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarabs are beetles, and like all insects they walk on six legs, hence the playful name.

clue.text: Unbeliever is at the assembly

indicators.note: an assembly puts parts together, so these letters are put together afresh

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nonbeliever turns up at a meeting, perhaps a church gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assembly' reads as a gathering such as school prayers, but it is the shuffle instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist rejects belief in any god, so is a person without religious faith.

clue.text: Bird making harsh sound

indicators.note: sound tells the solver to go by how the word is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: harsh means coarse or unrefined

explanation.surface: A bird gives a grating cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harsh sound' reads as the bird's call, but it says: a word for harsh, as spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruff is a wading bird whose males grow a frilly collar of feathers in the breeding season.

clue.text: Puzzle about right vehicle for a conductor

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
buses used to carry conductors who took fares

explanation.surface: A conundrum about the proper transport for an orchestra's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests music, but British buses once had a conductor collecting fares.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a puzzle in which pictures and symbols stand for words or syllables.

clue.text: Benevolent type throwing a coin in the water?

definitions.text: throwing a coin in the water?

blocks.note: first meaning: a kindly person who hopes things go well for others

blocks.clueFragment: throwing a coin in the water?
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: someone making a wish at a wishing well

explanation.surface: A kindly person tosses a coin into a fountain or pond.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, playful meaning: the phrase taken word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who hopes good things for others is kind, and the literal reading is a person wishing at a well.

clue.text: Idle, like many an awkward lout

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a large number
an oaf is a clumsy lout

explanation.surface: Many clumsy oafs are lazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To loaf is to lounge about doing nothing, which is what to idle means as a verb.

clue.text: A Shakespearian fly-by-night?

blocks.note: first meaning: the page to Armado in Love's Labour's Lost
second meaning: an insect that flies after dark

explanation.surface: An untrustworthy character from a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: A fly-by-night is a shady dealer, but read literally it is something that flies by night.
explanation.definitionFit: Moth is a page in Love's Labour's Lost, and the insect is mostly nocturnal, flitting about after dark.

clue.text: For the French, good attempts at making drums

blocks.note: bon is French for good
a go is a try, so goes are attempts

explanation.surface: French people have good tries at building percussion instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Bongos are a pair of small hand drums of Cuban origin, played between the knees.

clue.text: Nimbleness of soldier in Italy on manoeuvres

indicators.note: troops on manoeuvres move about in exercises, so the letters are moved about too

blocks.note: GI is an American soldier
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier on exercises in Italy shows how light on his feet he is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' only links the soldier and the country; all seven letters are shuffled together.
explanation.definitionFit: Agility is the quality of moving quickly and easily, the same thing as being light and quick on one's feet.

clue.text: Shape not uncommon for a carriage

indicators.note: uncommon means unusual, so the letters take an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fairly common shape for a horse-drawn vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not uncommon' looks like a double negative meaning fairly common, but 'not' is fodder and 'uncommon' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanhope is a light open one-seat horse-drawn vehicle, named after the clergyman for whom the first was built.

clue.text: Lie-abed in Pistol's world?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a shellfish that lies in a bed on the sea floor
second meaning: what Pistol in The Merry Wives of Windsor says the world is to him

explanation.surface: A lazybones lounging in the world of a Shakespearean swaggerer.
explanation.walkthrough: A lie-abed is a lazy late riser, but these shellfish literally lie in beds. Pistol says 'Why, then the world's mine oyster, which I with sword will open'.
explanation.definitionFit: The shellfish grows in beds on the seabed and is the thing Shakespeare's Pistol compares the world to.
